title: Proof
body_md:
$\kappa$ is convex on the set of row-stochastic matrices and $\kappa(I)=1$, so
$\kappa((1-\alpha)I+\alpha A)\le(1-\alpha)\kappa(I)+\alpha\kappa(A)$. At
$\alpha=\tfrac12$ this recovers the estimate of \citet{biccari2026}, obtained
there by the triangle inequality.

label: prop:exact

name: Exactness

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $i\neq j$ and write $d=A_{i\cdot}-A_{j\cdot}$, so $d_i=A_{ii}-A_{ji}$ and
$d_j=A_{ij}-A_{jj}$. Then
\begin{equation*}
\widetilde{A}_{i\cdot}-\widetilde{A}_{j\cdot}=(1-\alpha)(e_i-e_j)+\alpha d,
\end{equation*}
with $e_i$ the $i$-th canonical basis vector, whose coordinates are
$(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_i$ at position $i$, $-(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_j$ at position
$j$, and $\alpha d_k$ elsewhere. By the triangle inequality,
\begin{align*}
\tfrac12\bigl\|\widetilde{A}_{i\cdot}-\widetilde{A}_{j\cdot}\bigr\|_1
&=\tfrac12\Bigl(\bigl|(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_i\bigr|+\bigl|(1-\alpha)-\alpha d_j\bigr|
+\alpha\textstyle\sum_{k\neq i,j}|d_k|\Bigr)\\
&\le(1-\alpha)+\alpha\cdot\tfrac12\|d\|_1\;\le\;(1-\alpha)+\alpha\,\kappa(A).
\end{align*}
The first inequality holds term by term: since $1-\alpha>0$,
$\bigl|(1-\alpha)+\alpha d_i\bigr|\le(1-\alpha)+\alpha|d_i|$ with equality if and
only if $d_i\ge0$, and $\bigl|(1-\alpha)-\alpha d_j\bigr|\le(1-\alpha)+\alpha|d_j|$
with equality if and only if $d_j\le0$ (as $|x+y|=|x|+|y|$ if and only if
$xy\ge0$). So the first inequality is an equality if and only if $(i,j)$
satisfies~\eqref{eq:cond}, and the second if and only if $(i,j)$ attains
$\kappa(A)$.

If some $\kappa(A)$-attaining pair satisfies~\eqref{eq:cond},
equality holds throughout for it; since the chain bounds every pair,
$\kappa(\widetilde{A})=(1-\alpha)+\alpha\kappa(A)$.

Conversely, if
$\kappa(\widetilde{A})=(1-\alpha)+\alpha\kappa(A)$, equality holds throughout for any pair
attaining $\kappa(\widetilde{A})$, which has $i\neq j$ because this value is positive; as
$\alpha>0$, that pair attains $\kappa(A)$ and satisfies~\eqref{eq:cond}.

label: ex:swap
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:swap}
Let $A=\begin{psmallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{psmallmatrix}$, the two-token swap. Its
rows are disjoint, so $\kappa(A)=1$ and Lemma~\ref{prop:bound} gives only
the trivial bound $\kappa(\widetilde{A})\le1$. But
$\widetilde{A}=\tfrac12(I+A)=\begin{psmallmatrix}1/2&1/2\\1/2&1/2\end{psmallmatrix}$ has
identical rows, hence $\kappa(\widetilde{A})=0$: the residual destroys the entire
difference instead of preserving half of it. The condition fails at the only
attaining pair, since $A_{11}=0<1=A_{21}$.
head: environment
name: The bound can fail completely

title: Remark
body_md:
Condition~\eqref{eq:cond} says that each of the two extremal tokens attends to
itself at least as strongly as the other extremal token attends to it --- a
\emph{mutual self-dominance} of a pair that realises the coefficient (the pair
need not be unique; the condition asks this of some attaining pair, not of all).
The residual scales every row by $\alpha$ and adds mass $1-\alpha$ to its
diagonal entry; mutual self-dominance is precisely the condition under which,
for that pair, the added mass reinforces the existing difference between the two
rows rather than partially cancelling it. Example~\ref{ex:swap} is the opposite
extreme, where it cancels the difference entirely. The condition fails at a pair when one of its two
tokens receives more attention from the other than it pays itself --- a pattern
that an attention sink, receiving attention from many tokens, can produce when it
is one of the pair.
head: environment
name: Interpretation

label: rem:size
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:size}
The computation in the proof also bounds the size of a failure. For any pair
$(i,j)$ attaining $\kappa(A)$,
\[
0\le(1-\alpha)+\alpha\kappa(A)-\kappa(\widetilde{A})\le
\alpha\bigl[(A_{ji}-A_{ii})^+ + (A_{ij}-A_{jj})^+\bigr],
\]
and the bound on the gap is sharp: in Example~\ref{ex:swap} both sides equal $1$. A failure is therefore never larger than $\alpha$ times the total amount
by which the two inequalities of~\eqref{eq:cond} fail, and each of these amounts is
at most one attention entry. When attention is spread over many tokens its
entries are small, and so are its failures: uniformly random matrices with $256$
tokens (the uniform model below) fail condition~\eqref{eq:cond} about three times
in four, but at $\alpha=\tfrac12$ by a median gap of only $0.5\%$ of $\tfrac12\kappa(A)$.
